title: Spin Hall Effect in Collinear Ferromagnets from Spin-Group Symmetry
authors: Qing Zhang, Yizhuo Song, Jiahao Shentu, Jianting Dong, Jia Zhang
abstract: Magnetic materials support both time-reversal-even (T-even) and time-reversal-odd (T-odd) spin Hall currents, yet their underlying microscopic origins remain elusive. Here, we elucidate the spin Hall effect (SHE) in collinear ferromagnets by treating spin-orbit coupling (SOC) as a perturbation that breaks spin-group symmetry, thereby revealing how magnetic order activates distinct spin Hall response. To first order in SOC, we identify two dominant T-even SHE mechanisms: a magnetization-independent conventional contribution and a magnetization-dependent channel associated with anomalous Hall charge transport. At the same order, the leading T-odd magnetic spin Hall effect (MSHE) originates from the exchange interaction between the conventional spin current and the local magnetization. At second order in SOC, we further uncover a distinct T-odd planar spin Hall mechanism. Our spin-symmetry analysis is corroborated by first-principles calculations, which reveal a pronounced anisotropic magnetic spin Hall effect whose magnitude can be comparable to the T-even spin Hall conductivity (SHC) when the magnetic moment is tilted away from the principal crystallographic axes. These findings clarify the microscopic origins of the SHC in collinear ferromagnets and pave the way for ferromagnet-based spin current sources with versatile properties in spintronic applications.
summary: This work develops a comprehensive symmetry-based theory to uncover the microscopic origins of the Spin Hall Effect in ferromagnets. By treating spin-orbit coupling as a perturbation, the authors systematically derive distinct T-even and T-odd contributions to the spin Hall conductivity. The findings clarify how magnetic order dictates the magnitude and nature of these spin current sources for spintronic applications.
main_problem: The paper aims to elucidate the microscopic origins of the Spin Hall Effect (SHE) in collinear ferromagnets, specifically detailing how magnetic order activates distinct spin Hall responses.
main_result: It identifies multiple SHE mechanisms—including magnetization-independent and dependent T-even contributions, and a leading T-odd Magnetic Spin Hall Effect (MSHE)—whose origins are determined by the order of SOC perturbation.
method: The study employs symmetry analysis based on magnetic point-group symmetries and treats Spin-Orbit Coupling (SOC) as a systematic perturbation to expand the Spin Hall Conductivity (SHC).
model_or_system: The focus is on collinear ferromagnets, where SOC breaks spin-group symmetry. The theory is validated using first-principles calculations on materials like fcc ferromagnets.
key_observables: Spin Hall Conductivity ($\sigma_{ij}^k$), decomposed into Time-Reversal-Even (T-even) and Time-Reversal-Odd (T-odd) components, including the MSHE and Planar Spin Hall Effect (PSHE).
important_parameters: The strength of SOC ($\xi$) is treated as a small parameter for perturbation expansion; magnetization direction ($\mathbf{m}$) dependence is crucial.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes collinear ferromagnetism and develops the theory by treating SOC perturbatively up to second order in the expansion.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate spin current generation using an electric field, schematic interactions with magnetization $\mathbf{m}$, and show the calculated dependence of SHCs on SOC scaling factors and magnetization angle ($	heta$).
paper_structure: The paper develops a theoretical framework by applying symmetry constraints to expand the SHC in powers of SOC. It systematically identifies contributions at first order (T-even/T-odd) and second order (PSHE), validating these findings with first-principles calculations.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the rigorous use of symmetry group theory to decompose transport coefficients based on fundamental interactions (like SOC) provides a powerful theoretical template applicable across many areas of quantum physics.
